summary.title: On Coding, Ego and Attention
summary.one_liner: Ego-driven self-comparison and personal self-evaluation drain a programmer's attention, and treating the task as "out there" and adopting a beginner's mind can restore focus and learning.
keywords: h. a. dorfman mental abcs pitching
how to stop taking bugs personally
takeaways: Ego ties self-worth to work, causing performance tracking that distracts from the task.
Relative deprivation: self-comparison to peers can throttle effort regardless of ability.
Beginner's mind and treating mistakes as learning keep the learning curve from flattening.
Ask problem-focused questions ('Where is the bug?') instead of personal ones ('Did I cause the bug?') to keep the task at the center.
summary.summary: The author, a software engineer with over a decade of coding, argues that internal ego distraction hurts problem solving more than external distractions like phones or meetings. He draws on Malcolm Gladwell's STEM completion-rate example (relative deprivation), Zen shoshin (beginner's mind), and the scientific method to describe how expertise can cause motivated reasoning. His remedy is to ask only problem-focused questions and to create psychological distance so the task is "out there" rather than personal. The essay is reflective and opinion-based, with quotes from several authors supporting its points.
